topics.title: Cholinergic drugs and toxicity
points: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing cholinergic excess.
Organophosphate treatment: atropine for muscarinic effects plus pralidoxime to regenerate acetylcholinesterase (if given early).
Anticholinergic toxicity: hot, dry, flushed skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention, delirium.

cards.back: Irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so ACh builds up

questions.q: A farmer has miosis, salivation, bronchorrhea, and muscle fasciculations. Which drug reverses the fasciculations?
questions.explanation: Atropine only blocks muscarinic effects. Fasciculations are nicotinic, so pralidoxime (regenerating acetylcholinesterase) is needed.
Muscarinic blockade causes urinary retention, along with dry skin, mydriasis, and tachycardia.

topics.title: Glycolysis regulation
points: PFK-1 is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis.
PFK-1 is activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate.
Net yield of glycolysis is 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.
Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes hemolytic anemia because RBCs depend on glycolysis for ATP.

cards.front: Net ATP from glycolysis per glucose

questions.q: Which molecule most strongly activates PFK-1 in the fed state?
questions.explanation: Insulin raises fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, the most potent activator of PFK-1. Citrate and ATP inhibit it.

questions.q: A child has chronic hemolytic anemia and an enzyme defect in glycolysis. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
questions.explanation: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is the classic glycolytic cause of hemolysis. G6PD is in the pentose phosphate pathway, not glycolysis.
